notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 1 of your Six Foot Track Training Plan

Congratulations on entering the Six Foot Track Marathon. Here is some information to help you decide which level of the plan will make you the fittest, fastest and strongest on race day.

We have three different volume/difficulty levels of our Six FootTraining Plan. They are a reflection on how much time you have available to train, rather than a reflection on your goal time for the event. Some runners will be able to complete 45km in <5 hours following the intermediate plan, and other runners might take 6 hours 59 mins following the advanced plan.

You need to choose a level that you feel will be sustainable for the entire 16-week program. Your body needs to be able to comfortably cope with the volume without causing you illness or injuries, and your training schedule needs to be able to fit around all of the other aspects of your day-to-day life, such as work and family commitments.

You don’t have to stick to the same level for the entire plan (you have access to all three levels), you can go up or down levels depending on your time availability and how your body is coping with the volume. The key is consistency. You need to choose the level that allows you to run every week without needing any enforced rest.

Read the description in the Glossary Tab to decide whether you should follow the beginner, intermediate or advanced plan.

Stretching, Rolling and Strength

This week we are introducing a 3 minute morning stretching routine that you will be doing most days during the plan. This short and easy routine helps to stretch your lower back, glutes, quads, hip flexors, hips, knees, ankles and calf muscles. It will help you to remain injury free – so please try and stick with it every day you see it in the plan.

We are also introducing two different 10 minute bodyweight strength and stability routines (no equipment needed) and a 5 minute foam rolling and massage ball routine. To perform this you will need a foam roller and some sort of firm massage ball.

Training Plan

Make Sure You “Listen to your body”

This is an age-old cliché, but it has stood the test of time for good reason. It works! If something hurts when you are running, then don’t ignore it. Especially if it lingers for more than a few days. If possible, get it diagnosed by a health professional who runs. No one understands a runner’s body (and psyche) as well as a fellow runner. You will be able to resume training much quicker if you understand your injury and know what you can be doing to help your recovery

Do not try and stick to the weekly km if you do have an issue. Continuing to push through pain when you have a problem could stop you turning up on race day.

How to Use the Plan

To use the program properly, and to get the most benefit from it, you need to understand what all the session descriptions mean, so that you can use them to best effect in your training. You will see a number of shorthand descriptions which describe the details for that specific run. For example “Hill Reps” or “ELEV” or “UpDown Reps”

Go to the Glossary Tab for a detailed description of each training session

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
Running Technique

You need to start by working on the absolute foundation of what will lead to a successful race. Your running technique. It doesn’t matter how many stretches or exercises you do, if your running technique is not up to scratch, you will be much more likely to suffer a number of common running injuries and you will never reach your full potential.

Watch this video to learn how to run with good technique.

Strength Vs Stability

To be able to run and avoid injuries, you need to have good hip and pelvis stability. When working properly, the role of the stability muscles is to stabilise your skeleton and spine in the optimal position so the bigger, stronger muscles can develop force and create movement.

The ability to stand on one foot with your eyes closed for 60 seconds requires you to have good stability – We are going to test this in a minute .

I have often seen clients who can squat 100kg, or perform 100 sit-ups, but if they can’t stand on one foot for a minute, then the relative strength of their “movement” muscles is not going to help their running performance.

Test Your Stability Now

To get an understanding of stability, I want you to do this simple one minute test. Stand on one leg, close your eyes. Start counting in seconds 1, 2, 3…………

How long did you last until you had to put your foot down?.

If you made it to

- less than 10… You have a lot of work to do

- 10 – 30 ……. Still not good. Your lack of hip stability might cause some injuries

- 30 – 45 …….. Better, but still room for improvement

- 60 seconds …….. Great. Keep doing what you are doing

Record your results because we are going to test this again later in the plan

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
We’ve created an incredible weekly guide to help you manage your nutrition and hydration during training and on race day. Getting your nutrition right is just as crucial as completing your training and recovery sessions, so I encourage you to follow this plan closely.

This week’s focus is on “Just Eat Real Food” (JERF).

The JERF principle is a simple and effective approach to meal and snack choices, often referred to as a “whole foods” diet. It emphasizes eating foods that come straight from nature—out of the ground, off a tree, or from an animal—with minimal or no processing.

This approach ensures a nutrient-dense diet, which greatly benefits your overall health and well-being. It’s not just about the nutrients you’re consuming but also about avoiding harmful additives. Packaged foods often contain refined vegetable oils, chemicals, flavor enhancers, preservatives, and sugars that can disrupt your liver, metabolism, and hormones.

The foods you choose provide the essential building blocks for cell growth and DNA replication, directly impacting your muscles, ligaments, immune system, and overall vitality. Remember, the quality of your food is as important as the quality of your training and rest—together, they determine your performance and recovery.

After all, “you are what you eat.”

Your Homework This Week

The most effective way to improve your nutrition is through meal planning. Having healthy, ready-to-eat meals in your fridge puts you 90% ahead of the game.

Here’s how to get started:

- Plan Ahead: Dedicate a couple of hours over the weekend or one evening to plan your meals for the week.

- Shop Smart: Make a list based on your meal plan and shop accordingly—use online delivery services to save time.

- Prep & Cook: Prepare ingredients or cook some meals in advance so you’re always ready.

This week, write down your meals and aim to make a few healthier adjustments to your diet. Small changes can lead to big results!

notes.text:
Welcome to Week 2 of your Six Foot Track Training Plan

I hope you enjoyed your first week on the training plan. The first week included an overview into how to improve your running technique, some exercises to improve your core stability and we also introduced the 3 minute morning ritual.

Trail Vs Road – Do you have to do your long run on a trail?

I appreciate that not everyone will be able to run on a trail for all of their runs. Practice makes perfect. The best thing you can do to make yourself a stronger trail runner and to enjoy your race, is to run on trails which are similar to the terrain you expect to encounter on race day. Start doing some research now on the Six Foot course and try to find similar trails to train on. Firetrails with some big steep hills would be ideal, but also some runnable lumpy firetrail to mimic the second half of the Six Foot course.

If you find it difficult to get to a trail every weekend, you should try and plan a road route with a lot of hills, some stairs if possible, and mix up the terrain as much as possible e.g. road, grass, footpath, gravel etc.

What if you live in a flat area?

Are you training for a hilly trail event but you live on the flat? or you generally just struggle to find enough hills or stairs to train on? This is a common problem faced by runners, and it can cause quite a few issues on race day. Mostly cramping in the calves, hamstrings and adductor muscles.

Watch THIS VIDEO to learn how to use a Lunge-Squat-Lunge-Run Session is an easy way to help strengthen your legs for uphills, downhills and stairs no matter where you live. The idea is to use lunges and squats to increase the load on your leg muscles and also to get your joints and muscles working through a bigger range of motion. You then run 1km and repeat the squats and lunges – multiple times.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
Running Technique

Have you started to focus on your running technique yet? The sooner you learn to run with good technique the better. It is a VITAL component in the quest to staying injury free, and running faster.

In the video I refer to the importance of “cadence”. Cadence is the number of steps per minute you take when you are running. Running with the correct cadence is integral to good running form, and therefore also integral to staying injury-free. We will talk more about this as the weeks progress.

Uphill Running Technique

“Rolling Hills” feature a lot in this program, so now is the perfect time to learn how to run uphills efficiently.

Rolling hills is the term we use to describe running over a course that is consistently going up and downhill for the duration of your run. Plan ahead and identify a course that has a good amount of up and downhill. The hills don’t have to be steep but they should be as regular as possible throughout the course. Consider running a short hilly loop multiple times if you don’t have access to a long hilly route. You should average approximately 150m – 250m of vertical elevation per 10km of running on rolling hills.

The better your form when you run up the hills the faster you will be and the more energy you will conserve for later in the race.

Watch this video to learn what to focus on every time you are running uphill.

Accelerations

This week we are adding accelerations to the program. Accelerations are 20 to 40 second efforts building from an easy jog to a relaxed hard effort, and then easing back down to a jog again. Focus on running tall and keeping your cadence high and your strides short. Slowly walk or jog for 1 minute between accelerations. The purpose of accelerations is improve your leg speed, hip mobility, glute strength and your running technique. NB: They are not a sprinting or speed work session.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
Do you follow a weekly meal plan? Planning your meals ahead can significantly improve your food choices. Nutrition plays a vital role in your training, aiding recovery and strengthening your body.

This week, we’re focusing on the essential role of carbohydrates in your training.

Carbohydrates are the body’s primary energy source and the foundation of an endurance athlete’s diet. They are converted into glucose, which fuels your body and brain. Adequate glucose is crucial for maintaining focus, preventing mood swings, and avoiding sugar cravings.

Your carbohydrate intake should align with your activity level, as the body can only store a limited amount as glycogen. Excess carbs may be stored as fat and can cause insulin spikes, leading to fluctuating energy levels (hello, 3 PM slump!). This is more common with simple, processed carbs rather than complex, whole-food options.

So, how much should you eat, and what should it include?

For ultra-marathon training, most individuals need 3-6 grams of carbs per kilogram of body weight daily. For instance, a 70kg athlete may require between 210g to 420g of carbs per day, depending on body type and exercise intensity.

Focus on whole, unrefined complex carbohydrates like vegetables, fruits, and whole grains. However, not all carbs are created equal. Starchy carbs, such as potatoes, sweet potatoes, oats, rice, quinoa, and legumes, are higher in carbohydrates. If weight loss is a goal, limit starchy carbs to post-training meals, which we’ll explore further in the coming weeks.

For now, continue with your JERF (Just Eat Real Food) plan from last week, and work on making it a sustainable habit!

notes.text:
Running Technique

By now your running technique should be improving and the changes you have made should be starting to feel a bit more natural.

The three most important components of running technique are:

- Posture – stand up tall

- Cadence – 175 – 185 steps/minute

- Short Strides – foot landing close to under your body

Uphill Running Technique

This week we continue to focus on “Rolling Hills” in the training program – make sure you have nailed your uphill technique so that you are fast and efficient up the hills.

We are introducing some Up Down repeats this week. The purpose of UpDown Repeats is to improve your skill and speed at downhill running, and to strengthen your quad muscles which will help you to climb strongly after the downhill sections of the course. For these reps find a 1km section of your run route (road or fire trail) which is consistently undulating. Ideally on gentle inclines of 5 to 8 degrees. Run these reps at tempo effort

(NB: your pace will vary significantly depending on whether you are running uphill or downhill, but your level of effort or perceived exertion should be consistent during the rep).

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
This week, we’re focusing on the importance of protein in your diet and how much you should be consuming.

Alongside healthy carbohydrates, every meal and snack should include a source of protein. Here’s why protein is essential:

- Stabilises blood sugar levels

- Prevents energy crashes and curbs constant cravings

- Promotes satiety , making you feel fuller for longer

- Provides building blocks (amino acids) for muscles, hair, nails, brain cells, and immune system cells

- Supports hormone production , including essential ones like adrenaline

Which Foods Are Rich in Protein?

Animal-Based Proteins

These provide a complete amino acid profile, making them an excellent source of protein:

- Meat : Beef, lamb, turkey, chicken, pork

- Seafood : Fish, shellfish, prawns

- Eggs : Nature’s perfect protein

- Dairy : Milk, cheese, cream, yogurt

Plant-Based Proteins

Plant proteins are often incomplete, providing only some of the essential amino acids. To ensure your body gets all it needs, pair different plant proteins together—a practice known as “food combining.”

- Nuts and Seeds : Cashews, Brazil nuts, walnuts, pumpkin seeds, hemp, sunflower seeds, sesame seeds

- Legumes and Peas : Lentils, chickpeas, lima beans, kidney beans

- Grains : Oats, wheat germ, brown rice, quinoa, buckwheat

- Soy Products : Soybeans, tofu, edamame

Including a variety of these protein sources in your diet ensures you meet your nutritional needs while supporting overall health and energy.

When should you eat protein and how much is enough?

For optimal results, include a small amount of protein in every meal and snack. Most athletes require 1.2–1.5 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight .

For example, a 70 kg athlete needs about 85–105 grams of protein daily .

Protein Content Examples

- Meat : About 25–30% protein by weight. A 100 g portion of cooked chicken provides roughly 25 g of protein.

- Eggs : One large egg contains about 8 g of protein.

How to Track Your Protein Intake

To ensure you’re meeting your daily requirements:

- Track your meals for 1–2 weeks using an app like MyFitnessPal .

- Check labels on packaged foods such as nuts, grains, and dairy to see their protein content.

Key Tips for Protein Consumption

- Distribute protein evenly throughout the day across meals and snacks.

- The body can only absorb up to 40 grams of protein at a time , so consuming a large portion (e.g., a 300 g steak) at dinner won’t maximise your intake.

- Aim for 20–30 grams per meal , with the remainder coming from snacks.

Your Homework for the Week

Set up a free account on MyFitnessPal or a similar app to log your meals. This will help you understand your eating patterns and how they impact your performance.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 4 of your Six Foot Track Training Plan – A recovery week.

Good news.

This week is a recovery week in the 16-week program, so the long run is shorter and the Thursday session is easier. By reducing the volume and intensity of the training this week, it will allow your body a chance to recover from the fatigue and tight muscles which will have been building up over the last three weeks.

The recovery week will set you up to be fresh and raring to go for the next build phase of the program.

Despite the reduced running volume, this is NOT A REST WEEK . You need to continue with the same number of runs per week and be just as diligent (if not, more so) with your body maintenance sessions.

A week of complete rest will probably leave you feeling tired and sluggish and less motivated to get back into the training next week. The aim of the recovery week is to keep your body and your brain used to running, whilst still logging some all-important km’s in the training diary.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
We have focused on running technique for the last three weeks. Make sure you keep it “front of mind” during every run. Bad habits have a tendency to start creeping in as you become fatigued. Towards the end of the long run is when you are most likely to revert back to over-striding and dropping your cadence.

One strategy to combat this drop in form is to have short walking breaks.

You might be two hours into the long run, for example, feeling tired and starting to slump down and overstride.

If you walk for a couple of minutes then start running again, you will be more likely to be able to maintain a good posture and cadence. You can have as many walking breaks as you need to throughout the run as they won’t have a negative effect on your endurance, and they will ultimately increase your chances of being able to stick with this program.

Keep this little mantra running through your head, especially when you are tired “stand up tall, short steps, stand up tall, short steps, stand up tall . . . “

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
Last week, you should have set up an account with MyFitnessPal or a similar app to start tracking your protein and carbohydrate intake.

This week, we’re shifting our focus to Healthy Fats —why they matter and where to find them.

Why Are Healthy Fats Important?

Healthy fats are essential for your body and can actually help with weight loss. They keep you feeling full and satisfied, reducing the likelihood of overeating. Fat is vital for:

- Building cell membranes.

- Hormone production.

- Transporting and absorbing key vitamins (A, D, E, and K).

Incorporating Healthy Fats

Every meal should include a small amount of fat. This is simple if you’re following the “JERF” principle and meeting your protein goals, as fats are often naturally present in protein-rich foods.

An easy way to add fat is by drizzling olive oil over your vegetables or salads. Many athletes also increase their fat intake with MCT oil (from coconut oil), commonly added to coffee to create “bulletproof coffee.” MCT oil is an excellent source of healthy fat.

Omega-3 Fatty Acids: Essential for Your Body

Unlike other fats, the body cannot produce omega-3 fatty acids on its own—they must come from your diet. These essential fatty acids are crucial for overall health.

Sardines are a powerhouse for Omega-3! While tinned tuna contains around 150mg of Omega-3 per serving, sardines pack a massive 2900mg per serving—nearly 20 times more.

Health experts recommend 250mg–500mg of EPA/DHA daily. Eating sardines twice a week easily covers this requirement. If sardines aren’t your go-to, give them a try—you might be surprised. My favourite way to enjoy them is in a salad, but they’re also great on sourdough toast or straight from the tin as a snack.

Examples of Healthy Fats

- Oils: Olive oil, coconut oil, flaxseed oil, and nut oils.

- Animal fats: Chicken skin, lard, egg yolks.

- Fatty fish: Salmon, mackerel, sardines.

- Full-fat dairy: Butter, yogurt, ricotta, full-fat milk, cheese, and halloumi.

- Nuts and seeds: Cashews, walnuts, sunflower seeds, pepitas, chia, hemp, and linseeds.

- Fruits: Avocado and coconut.

Make healthy fats a consistent part of your meals, and your body will thank you with improved energy, recovery, and overall performance!

notes.text:
Naked Running Band

The Naked Running Band is my favourite running accessory of all time. It can carry a lot of stuff and it works very well in tandem with a vest / pack.

Naked Running Bands are great for carrying your poles and race number, and they provide extra capacity for carrying water and food.

These bands are perfect for both training and racing.

I can comfortably carry 1 litre of water, my phone, a snake bandage, a survival blanket and a bunch of gels without the band bouncing, and without the need for training with a vest / pack. I use this on training runs and shorter races.

Watch this video to work out how to measure yourself for the correect size

notes.text:
Welcome to Week 5 of your Six Foot Track Training Plan

Training Advice

We are now getting into some bigger training weeks.

The combination of longer weekend runs and either a tempo run or hill repeats sessions during the week is putting your body under more stress. If you are consistent with the stretches and exercises, and you are following the running program so that there are not any big jumps in volume, then your body should tolerate the increased load and you will become stronger and faster.

If you have a few niggles starting to appear that you are worried about, here are some strategies you should use to help keep them under control.

Adopt the “little and often” philosophy . Breaking your weekly distance into shorter but more regular runs will be easier for your body to cope with.

- In an ideal training program the long run is important, but it is counter-productive if you then have to miss 2-3 days of training because of it.

- For example – you could split the total volume of your long run between Saturday and Sunday, or Sunday and Monday – so that your overall weekly volume remains similar, but you don’t have the extra stress of a really long run for your body to cope with.

Speedwork – Don’t do any! Whether it is hill reps, tempo park runs or even hill reps. If you have got a niggle then leave any speed sessions out of your program until the niggle has settled.

- You will get a lot more benefit out of being able to continue to train than you will from persevering with speedwork and potentially making an injury worse.

Self Massage – sit down every evening and massage your sore bits (usually calves, feet, ITBs)

- A foam roller can be helpful for I TBs, quads and calves

- A tennis ball or golf ball can be useful for the sole of your foot (through the arch of your foot – not over the heel or the bony bits near the ball of your foot)

- A trigger point ball can be useful for your glute muscles

Ice – Icing a swollen achilles tendon, an inflamed ITB, or a painful foot can be a great way to help settle your symptoms in time to be able to run again the next day.

- Use ice cubes in a plastic bag NOT one of those blue gel packs. If ice cubes are not possible then frozen peas will (just) suffice. Ice cubes stay at a constant temperature (0 degrees) until they have melted. Ice packs usually start off too cold (-7 degrees) and warm up too quickly, so they can give you a nasty “freezer burn” and they don’t stay cold long enough to be effective.

Stretching – stretching your calf muscles for example can help to reduce the tension in your Achilles tendon. Stretching your glute muscles can help to reduce ITB and knee symptoms.

Most importantly – “Listen to your Body” – if you are concerned about a niggle or an injury during your training, then get it diagnosed by a trusted health care professional and take some proactive steps towards managing it and getting treatment if required.

Do not try and stick to the weekly km if you do have an issue. Continuing to push through pain when you have a problem could stop you turning up on race day.

Strength and Stability Workouts

This week we are stepping up to some harder strength and stability exercises. They are now 20 minute workouts and they include a kettlebell, skipping rope and you need a bench or a step for doing steps ups. We will also be adding some plyometric (jumping) exercises.

Try and get hold of a kettlebell that is somewhere between 2kg and 8kg (depending on your upper body strength) for these workouts.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
Cadence

Cadence is the number of steps per minute you take. There is a bit of controversy around whether there is a specific number you should aim for. The “golden number” of 180 – is often quoted.

I am a huge believer that 180 is the gold standard and something that you should all ultimately be aiming for.

What should you do to improve your cadence?

The best way to work on improving your cadence is to use a metronome. You can buy a small, clip-on, digital metronome that is perfect for the purpose, or if you run with your phone, you can download a metronome app and use that. Set the metronome to the appropriate beat, and run in time with the beeps (one foot landing each time you hear a beep).

- We have digital metronomes available in our shop which are perfect for helping you regulate your cadence.

- A few watches now have built in metronomes – so check to see if your watch can be your metronome.

- There are a lot of free metronome Apps available for both Apple and Android phones which are also perfect for the job.

Follow these steps to make sure you do it accurately and safely

- Measure your cadence. During the middle of a normal training run, count your steps on one foot (i.e just your left) for a minute on a section of flat ground. Double it. This will give you your cadence. Repeat this several times over several runs to work out an accurate average.

- It is difficult to increase your cadence by more than 10 steps/minute in any one go. If your cadence is 160, for example, you should set your metronome to 170 and get used to that for a month, before increasing it further to 180.

- Continue using the metronome for as long as you need to until 180 becomes your natural / subconscious gait pattern.

There are two common, but temporary repercussions of increasing your cadence that you should be aware of

- It will increase your heart rate. Expect to breathe a bit harder, and get tired a bit quicker than you have been used to. Your cardio-vascular system will adjust over time, but expect it to take 2-3 months to fully adjust.

- Your calf muscles will probably do more work, and get tighter. As our stride gets shorter, our foot usually lands flatter, which uses the calf muscle more. Your calf muscles will get stronger with time, but some extra stretching and/or foam rolling will help during the transition.

I have been working as a physiotherapist treating running injuries for nearly thirty years, and I have spent the last sixteen years working with thousands of runners to improve their technique and reduce their injuries.

Cadence has been one of the most effective and beneficial changes most of those runners have made .

If you want to take your running to the next level, and you haven’t yet focused on your cadence, make sure you do. It can transform your running.

If you like running with music, it is possible to use an App to play music at a certain number of beats per minute. It is much harder though, to follow the rhythm of music than it is to follow the simple beat of a metronome, so I would highly recommend using a simple metronome App initially, and once you have become accustomed to the higher cadence and it feels natural, then you could switch back to running with music.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
A common challenge for athletes, especially during peak training phases, is maintaining a strong immune system. To protect yourself from colds, flu, and viruses, it’s essential to fuel your body with the right nutrition and resources.

Endurance running can weaken the immune system due to increased oxidative stress. To combat this, it’s crucial to incorporate more antioxidant-rich foods into your diet. These help neutralize free radicals, restore balance, and protect your mitochondria—the powerhouse of energy production—from damage.

Key Antioxidant Nutrients:

- Vitamin C, Vitamin E, Vitamin A, and CoQ10

Antioxidant Food Sources:

- Vegetables: Capsicum, broccoli, dark leafy greens, tomatoes, and sweet potatoes.

- Fruits: Berries, citrus fruits, papaya, and kiwi.

- Beverages: Green tea and matcha tea.

- Protein Sources: Organ meats (e.g., liver, heart), oily fish (sardines, mackerel, salmon).

- Nuts & Seeds: A variety of nuts and seeds.

Are You Including These Daily?

Aim for at least 5 servings of vegetables and 1-2 servings of fruit per day. These not only provide essential carbohydrates but are also packed with nutrients. If you’re struggling to meet this goal, try smoothies! Blend fruit, vegetables, matcha powder, and a handful of nuts or seeds for a quick nutrient boost.

If organ meats aren’t appealing, look for minced meat blends that include them—you won’t even notice! Alternatively, add a high-quality pâté to your meals.

Supplementing Antioxidants

Many athletes find antioxidant supplements helpful, particularly if their diet lacks these nutrients. Consult a qualified nutritionist or naturopath to choose the best supplements for your needs and maximize their benefits.

Your Task This Week:

Focus on consciously including 5 servings of vegetables daily . If you’re already doing this, keep it up! If not, start making small improvements to align your diet with your training goals. Your nutrition should complement all the hard work you’re putting into your training.

notes.text:
Welcome to Week 6 of your Six Foot Track Training Plan

This week, we’re continuing to build your training volume and introducing stair repeats to improve your climbing strength.

For the stair session, try to find the longest, most convenient staircase available — the more steps, the better. Focus on hiking the stairs rather than running them. Hiking activates your calves, glutes, and quads in a slightly different way, and this session is all about strengthening those muscles for the long haul.

Even though the Six Foot course doesn’t feature a huge amount of stairs (only the initial descent down Nellies Glen), this type of training is a safe and highly effective way to develop trail-specific strength and resilience. Strong uphill hikers make strong trail runners.

When doing these stair reps you can hike up and then run or walk slowly back down the stairs to recover. Repeat for the stated duration on the training plan.

Your pace for each stair rep should stay consistent throughout the session. Don’t start so fast that you can’t maintain your pace.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
Stair Running Technique

Watch this video on Stair Running Technique to learn how to run efficiently both up and down stairs. We are introducing some stair repeats into the program this week.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
By now, you should be eating plenty of vegetables, tracking your food intake, and feeling healthier than ever! The next step is to focus on timing your nutrition to ensure your body gets what it needs when it needs it most.

This week, we’re highlighting the importance of post-training meals and how to optimize them.

Why Is Your Post-Training Meal Crucial?

After training, your body needs proper nutrition to:

- Replenish muscle glycogen stores.

- Stimulate protein synthesis for muscle repair.

- Reduce cortisol levels (to avoid adrenal fatigue).

It’s essential to consume this meal within 45 minutes after your workout, especially if it was a tough session lasting more than 60 minutes. The right combination of carbohydrates and protein is key:

- Carbs : Replenish glycogen stores and reduce cortisol, both critical for recovery and weight control.

- Protein : Repairs muscles and supports your immune system.

How Much Should You Eat?

Your needs depend on your body weight, training intensity, and goals. Here’s a general guide:

- Carbs : ~1 gram per kilogram of body weight (or 1.5–2 grams after long sessions).

- Protein : ~⅓ of your body weight in grams.

For example:

- A 60kg athlete would need 60g carbs and 20g protein after training.

- For sessions under 60 minutes, aim for 40g carbs and 10–15g protein .

What Should You Eat?

Choose nutrient-dense options to maximize recovery:

- Carbohydrates : Fruit, starchy vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds.

- Proteins : Eggs, fish, lean meat, dairy.

Post-Training Meal Ideas

Breakfast Options:

- Fruit with yogurt, topped with nuts, seeds, or muesli.

- Eggs and toast with spinach or avocado.

- Smoothies with fruit, milk, nuts, or seeds.

- Frittata with potato/sweet potato and corn.

- Porridge made with milk, topped with fruit, yogurt, and a drizzle of honey.

Dinner Options:

- Chicken stir-fry with brown rice.

- Steak with sweet potato and greens.

- Grilled fish with a buckwheat, beetroot, and spinach salad.

- Homemade burgers with a large leafy green salad.

Your Task This Week

Keep up the excellent work and start experimenting with your post-run meals. Track what you eat and note how you feel the next day. This will help you discover the meals that work best for your recovery and performance.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 7 of your Six Foot Track Training Plan

We are increasing volume again this week.

notes.text:
At this stage in your training plan, you might find yourself feeling constantly hungry !

This week, we’re focusing on how to increase your calorie intake to meet the demands of your training without risking weight gain.

Why Calorie Balance Matters

As your training load increases, so do your energy needs. Ensuring your body gets the right nutrients and hydration is essential for maintaining energy levels, supporting effective training, and keeping your immune system strong.

By sticking to the JERF principle (Just Eat Real Food), you’ll be consuming a nutrient-dense diet. Take a moment to review what we’ve covered in previous weeks about healthy carbs, protein, and fats. Make a conscious effort to include protein at every meal and hit your daily protein target.

Avoiding “Hanger” and Weight Gain

With your metabolism revving and time spent training increasing, it’s easy to grab packaged snacks or fast food when hunger strikes—leading to unintentional weight gain. Remember, 80% of weight control comes from what you eat, with only 20% influenced by exercise.

To avoid this, prioritize:

- Meal planning and prep : Dedicate time to shopping and preparing meals to stay on track.

- Smart snacking : Focus on nutrient-dense snacks to avoid processed foods.

- Carbohydrate timing : Post-training meals : Include starchy carbs to aid recovery. Other meals : Focus on quality protein, healthy fats, and plenty of “above-ground” vegetables (e.g., leafy greens, broccoli, cauliflower).

- Post-training meals : Include starchy carbs to aid recovery.

- Other meals : Focus on quality protein, healthy fats, and plenty of “above-ground” vegetables (e.g., leafy greens, broccoli, cauliflower).

Remember: You can’t outrun a bad diet.

Your Homework This Week

- Track your food and calorie burn : Use tools like MyFitnessPal or your running watch to monitor your intake and energy expenditure.

- Stick with your progress : Continue eating lots of vegetables, meeting your protein goals, and noting what works for you.

- Be mindful of calorie balance : Ensure you’re eating enough to fuel your training while keeping weight in check.

With a bit of planning and awareness, you’ll be able to meet the demands of your training and keep progressing toward your goals!

notes.text:
Welcome to Week 8 of your Six Foot Track Training Plan – your second recovery week

Good news. This week is a recovery week in the 16 week program and you are now half way through your training. Only 8 weeks to go!

This week the the long run is shorter and the Thursday session is easier. By reducing the volume and intensity of the training this week, it will allow your body a chance to recover from the fatigue and tight muscles which will have been building up over the last three weeks.

The recovery week will set you up to be fresh and raring to go for the next phase of the program.

Despite the reduced running volume, this is NOT A REST WEEK .

You need to continue with the same number of runs per week and be just as diligent (if not, more so) with your body maintenance sessions. A week of complete rest will probably leave you feeling tired and sluggish and less motivated to get back into the training next week. The aim of the recovery week is to keep your body and your brain used to running, whilst still logging some all-important km’s in the training diary.

Try and do the 3 minute morning ritual every day this week. This will really help keep niggles at bay.

Rest and Sleep

Getting adequate sleep is an extremely important part of your training program. This is often overlooked when training for a specific event, especially when the training load increases – as extra training hours are often prioritised over sleep – this is not a good strategy and often ends up compromising the immune system or contributing to fatigue.

Your training program includes at least one rest day per week, it is vital that you allow your body rest – as this is when the muscles repair and re-build. Resting also allows hormones such as cortisol to recover and decrease – which is vital for weight management and ensuring that you do not suffer from over training syndrome.

Activities such as swimming, light yoga, having a sauna or getting a sports massage, are excellent choices for rest days.

If you struggle to fall asleep at night, try going to bed an hour earlier. Developing a pre-bedtime routine can also help, for example -2 hours prior to bed – finish eating and avoid screens, enjoy a cup of herbal tea, and read a book to calm your mind and help you fall asleep.

Most athletes need 7-8 hours sleep per night.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
This week, we’re diving into the critical role of daily hydration as your training volume increases.

Why Is Hydration So Important?

Water makes up about 60% of your body weight and is vital for nearly every bodily function, including:

- Digestion, absorption, and nutrient transport.

- Waste elimination.

- Temperature regulation.

- Supporting countless chemical processes.

Dehydration can negatively impact your performance, leaving you with headaches, fatigue, and mental fog.

How Much Water Do You Need?

A good daily guideline is 35ml per kilogram of body weight . For example:

- A 70kg person: 70 × 35 = 2,450ml/day .

Don’t worry—this total includes all fluids (yes, even coffee and tea count!) and water from foods, particularly fruits and vegetables, which are 70–95% water .

To simplify: aim for 10 glasses per day (1 glass = ~250ml).

- Example: Two coffees (~250ml each) already contribute to two glasses!

If you struggle to stay hydrated, invest in high-quality, BPA-free bottles and keep them with you—whether in the car, at your desk, or on the go.

How to Check Your Hydration

The easiest way to monitor hydration is by checking your urine:

- Pale straw colour : You’re hydrated.

- Darker with strong odor : You’re dehydrated. Note: Urine is often slightly darker in the morning but should lighten as the day progresses.

Hydration During Exercise

Exercise increases water loss through sweat and respiration. On average, you lose 700–850ml per hour of exercise.

It’s unlikely you’ll drink this much during your session, so it’s essential to rehydrate consistently throughout the day rather than all at once.

Sports Drinks: Helpful or Not?

Sports drinks provide water, electrolytes (sodium and potassium), and carbohydrates (sugar). However:

- The average 600ml bottle contains as much sugar as a soft drink!

- If you’re exercising for less than 60 minutes , water alone is sufficient.

If you’re aiming to lose weight, sports drinks aren’t the best option.

Replacing Electrolytes

For most people, a balanced diet covers your electrolyte needs, especially if you exercise up to an hour 3–4 times a week .

However, if you’re training for 90+ minutes or endurance events , you’ll need to replace lost sodium, potassium, and magnesium. Options include:

- Electrolyte products without added sugar.

- Adding good-quality salt to your meals or water.

This Week’s Focus

- Monitor your daily water intake and aim for your target.

- Pay attention to your urine colour to gauge hydration.

- If you’re training for extended periods, start thinking about replenishing electrolytes effectively.

Stay consistent with your hydration habits, and your body will thank you both during training and recovery!

Your Shoes

With only 8 weeks until your race, if you are thinking of changing your shoes or getting new ones now would be a good time to get them. You ideally need to test them on 2 or 3 long runs to make sure they are comfortable and that they are not going to cause blisters.

Welcome to Week 9 of your Six Foot Track Training Plan

We are building the volume again this week.

This would be a great week to do your long run on the Six Foot course if you can.

Doing a recce on the course will help you mentally prepare for what is coming. It is also a great way to get in the training miles you need.

Please remember, if you feel like you haven’t done enough training, or for some reason you have missed one or two of the long runs in the last few weeks – don’t try and play catch up by adding additional distance.

You should never increase your volume by more than 10% in a week. This is much more likely to lead to injury. Stick with the distances recommended in the training program, rather than trying to squeeze in one more long run.

For your long run this week, make sure you are practicing your race nutrition. This week we will go into detail on the amount of fuel your body needs during a 4 hour training run.

Mental Training

I think it is important to understand the role your mental stamina plays in training and racing for a 50km event.

Most of you will have reached a point in a race where you can no longer maintain your pace. It happens in 5km races, and it definitely happens in ultra marathons. In fact, it happens so frequently in ultra marathons that it has a name. “Hitting the wall”

How many of you have hit the so-called wall?

That point in a race where you feel exhausted: your legs are tired, your feet hurt and you feel like the only way that you’ll make it to the finish line without dying is to either slow down, walk, or maybe even crawl

I think there is a strong case to suggest that training our brains will make us faster. Long training runs and speed workouts help us mentally prepare our brains. They teach us that we can keep going even when tired.

On your next run I recommend thinking about some strategies you can use to keep going when the going gets tough.

Ideas like

- spend 1km thanking a person that helped you make your race. Then someone else the next 1km and so on.

- sing your favourite song in your head to help stop any negative thoughts creeping in.

- Use the alphabet and starting at the letter A, think of a word about why you love trail running. For example, atmosphere, bananas, cheering …

Strength and Stability Workouts

This week we are stepping up again to some harder strength and stability exercises. They are now 30 minute workouts and they include a kettlebell, skipping rope, a bench or a step, plyometric (jumping) exercises and a medicine ball.

You don’t absolutely need the medicine ball to complete these workouts, you could use your kettlebell, but a 3-5kg medicine ball would be very helpful.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
This week, we’re focusing on fuelling and hydration during your long runs to ensure your body gets what it needs to perform at its best. Practicing your nutrition strategy now is crucial—making changes close to race day is not recommended. Feeling confident in your plan will help calm pre-race nerves and set you up for success.

Training Runs up to 90 Minutes

If you’re following a nutrient-dense diet, additional fuelling may not be necessary for runs under 90 minutes. However, some runners benefit from a small amount of fuel beforehand. Listen to your body—choose simple carbohydrates, low in protein and fat.

Hydration: Water during this distance is beneficial.

Training Runs Between 90 Minutes and 3 Hours

For runs in this range, aim to consume 30–45 grams of carbohydrates per hour (or 120–180 calories), depending on body weight, pace, and experience.

Pro Tip: Always pair carbs with water to improve absorption. Use a 10% carb solution as a guideline—for 45g carbs/hour, drink ~450ml water/hour.

Carbohydrate Examples:

- Gels : Most contain 20–30g carbs—check the label and consume with water, not sports drinks.

- Natural options : 5 dates (30g carbs), 1 banana (25–30g carbs).

- Bars or sports drinks : Convenient options—read labels to determine carb content.

Training Runs Between 4 and 12 Hours

For ultra-endurance runs, energy comes from a mix of carbohydrates and fat , with carbs playing a critical role in accessing fat stores for fuel.

Think of fat as logs on a fire and carbs as the kindling—you need carbs to keep the fire burning. Without them, the fire (your energy) will go out, leading to “bonking” or “hitting the wall.”

Key Fuelling Tips:

- Start fuelling within the first 30 minutes . Don’t wait until fatigue sets in.

- Consume 45–60g carbs/hour , and up to 120g/hour for some runners. Fuel every 15–20 minutes .

Carbohydrate Sources:

- Gels or sports drinks: Easiest for quick absorption.

- Solid foods: Ideal for longer runs, especially if gels become hard to tolerate. Opt for low-fiber, high-GI options: Bananas, energy bars, white bread with peanut butter or honey. Mini pancakes, baked potatoes with salt. Avoid sugary snacks (e.g., lollies, cola) until the final 60–90 minutes.

- Bananas, energy bars, white bread with peanut butter or honey.

- Mini pancakes, baked potatoes with salt.

- Avoid sugary snacks (e.g., lollies, cola) until the final 60–90 minutes.

Adding Protein:

For long runs, a small amount of protein can help prevent central nervous system fatigue. This can be found in energy bars or peanut butter sandwiches.

Caffeine may also be beneficial for maintaining focus and energy levels.

Example Fuelling Plan for a 6-Hour Run:

- 50g carbs/hour = 300g total carbs = 12 gels or 12 scoops of Tailwind.

- Mix and match gels, drinks, bars, and solid food for variety.

Hydration

Staying hydrated is crucial, but it’s just as important to avoid overhydration. Both dehydration and overhydration (hyponatremia) can significantly impact performance.

Sweat Rate and Hydration Needs:

- Average sweat loss: 600–750ml/hour (varies with pace, temperature, and individual factors).

- Perform a sweat test during a 1-hour run to determine your specific needs.

Why Hydration Matters: Water helps keep your blood flowing efficiently, delivering oxygen and sodium to your heart, lungs, and muscles. Dehydration thickens your blood, making your heart work harder, which affects performance.

Electrolytes

During long runs, you lose salts (mainly sodium) through sweat. Replacing electrolytes is essential to:

- Enhance hydration by allowing water to enter cells.

- Reduce the risk of hyponatremia and muscle cramps.

Sources of Electrolytes:

- Salt capsules (available at sports stores).

- Electrolyte drinks, gels, or chews (check labels for added sodium).

- Adding good-quality salt to meals or drinks.

This Week’s Focus

- Start practicing your fuelling and hydration strategy during long runs.

- Experiment with different fuel sources and timing to find what works best for you.

- Monitor hydration and consider a sweat test to tailor your fluid intake.

Practicing now will help you feel confident and prepared for race day, ensuring your nutrition and hydration become second nature.

This week you have one of the longest runs in the whole program, and it is an important session, but it is also important that you aren’t out on your feet for so long that it will cause you too much fatigue to be able to train properly next week. notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
Finding the Best Fuel for You

This week, we’re revisiting race nutrition to help you refine your fuelling strategy for long runs.

Most runners require 45–60 grams of carbohydrates per hour during long runs. For some, this may increase to up to 120 grams per hour , but you’ll need to experiment during training to determine what works best. Your fuel can come from sports drinks, gels, chews, bars, or real food.

How to Calculate Your Fuel

- Read Labels: Check the carbohydrate content of your chosen products.

- Space It Out: Your gut can only absorb a limited amount of carbs at once. Divide your intake into 2–3 servings per hour .

- Set Alarms: Use your watch to remind you to eat every 20–30 minutes .

What Fuel Works Best?

- Single Source vs. Mixed Sources: Some runners prefer sticking to one type of fuel (e.g., gels), while others benefit from a combination (e.g., gels, chews, and bars).

- Training Your Gut: Part of training is teaching your gut to absorb carbs while running. If you’re new to endurance sports, start with smaller amounts and gradually increase.

Signs You Need More Fuel

If you’re hitting the wall or “bonking” during training, you’re likely not consuming enough carbohydrates. Experiment with your intake to find the right balance—enough to keep you energized without causing gastrointestinal distress.

Gels: A Convenient Option

Gels are popular for their ease of use, especially during ultra-distance events. However, they must be consumed with at least 250ml of water to ensure proper absorption and avoid stomach discomfort.

Flavour Fatigue

During ultra-endurance events lasting 15+ hours, you may experience flavour fatigue , where certain foods (like gels) become unpalatable. To avoid this, have backup options ready, such as:

- Savory options: Chicken noodle soup or minestrone at checkpoints.

- Real foods: Bars, bananas, or sandwiches can provide variety and relief from sweet, packaged products.

This Week’s Homework

- Adjust Your Strategy: Continue refining your race nutrition plan, noting what works and what doesn’t.

- Experiment: Test different fuels, brands, and flavours.

- Document: Record your findings so you feel confident and prepared for race day.

The key to success is trial and error—building a strategy that keeps you energized and prevents “flavour fatigue” will make all the difference on race day!

notes.text:
Welcome to Week 11 of your Six Foot Track Training Plan

This is another big volume week.

This week your long run should be all about putting into practice everything you have learnt. Try and find some trail terrain that is similar to your race course for your long run. Once again I am recommending a maximum run time, so you should either run the recommended distance, or the max time. Whichever one is shorter.

If you are tempted to run further for your long run this week, I strongly recommend you don’t. In my experience most runners err on the side of too much training, rather than too little, and without knowing it, they start the race in a state of fatigue.

There is a trade off between the fitness, strength and endurance you get from your long runs, and the fatigue, niggles and recovery time required before you can train properly again.

I think that the cut-off is around 5-6 hrs of running. If you spend more than 6 hours running, then the balance of fitness Vs recovery swings too much towards recovery, and you lose out overall in terms of fitness as a result of having to spend too much time recovering. 6hrs of running might mean 60km – 65km for an elite level athlete, and it might mean “only” 30km-35km for a less experienced runner.

Please remember, if you feel like you haven’t done enough training, or for some reason you have missed one or two of the long runs in the last few weeks – don’t try and play catch up by adding additional distance

Your Biggest Priority – Don’t get injured!

With less than 6 weeks until race day, your single biggest priority is to stay in one piece.

If you have any niggles or injuries you are worried about, now is the time to get them addressed. Take the following steps:

- Swap some runs for some cross training sessions, so that you can maintain your fitness whilst dealing with the injury.

- See your trusted health care professional – (physio, sports-massage therapist, osteo etc). Get the injury diagnosed, and learn what you can do to help it.

- Prioritise your stretching and/or foam rolling exercises every day to reduce some of the running-related tension in your muscles.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
Race Day Nutrition Guide

Proper nutrition on race day is essential to help you perform your best and avoid unnecessary discomfort. The key is preparation—know exactly what you’ll eat and drink, and practice it during training to ensure your plan works for you. Here’s a breakdown to guide you through race-day fuelling.

Pre-Race Breakfast

On race morning, nerves may make eating difficult, but breakfast is essential. Stick to foods you’ve practiced with during training—race day is not the time to try anything new.

Timing: Eat 2 hours before the race for optimal digestion. Composition:

- Focus on carbohydrates (1–2 grams of carbs per kg of body weight).

- Low in fiber, fat, and protein to minimize the risk of stomach issues.

Examples:

- 30 grams of carbs: 1 medium banana 2 slices of white bread 1.5 crumpets 4–6 dates 2 tbsp honey 1 gel (check the label for 20–30g carbs) Sports drink (check the label)

- 1 medium banana

- 2 slices of white bread

- 1.5 crumpets

- 4–6 dates

- 2 tbsp honey

- 1 gel (check the label for 20–30g carbs)

- Sports drink (check the label)

Avoid: Sports drinks in the hour before the race—sip water instead. If needed, consume a gel 10–15 minutes before the start for a quick energy boost.

Fuelling During the Race

By race day, you should have practiced your fuelling strategy and know exactly what you’ll consume. Do not wait until the night before—or worse, “wing it” on the day.

Carbohydrates: Stick to your planned intake to maintain energy levels and avoid hitting the wall.

Hydration

Staying hydrated is crucial but varies greatly depending on your sweat rate and race-day conditions.

Sweat Rate:

- Calculate your hourly sweat rate during training.

- If unsure, aim for 600–750ml per hour as a general guideline.

Hydration Tips:

- Faster runners: Drink small amounts regularly at aid stations to avoid dehydration.

- Slower runners: Be cautious of overhydrating, which can lead to hyponatremia (low sodium levels). To prevent this, consume electrolytes during the race to balance sodium levels.

Post-Race Recovery

Pay attention to your nutrition within the 45–60 minutes after finishing.

Goal: Replenish glycogen stores (carbs) and promote muscle recovery (protein). Carb:Protein Ratio: Aim for 4:1 .

Options:

- Sports recovery drinks or bars (portable and convenient).

- If accessible, a balanced meal containing carbs and protein.

Final Tips for Race Day Success

- Practice: Make your race-day plan part of your training routine.

- Prepare: Have backup options for unexpected issues or dislikes.

- Stay Consistent: Stick to what works—race day is not the time for experiments.

A well-planned nutrition and hydration strategy can make all the difference in your performance and recovery.

Welcome to Week 12 of your Six Foot Track Training Plan – the final recovery week

This week is the last recovery week in the 16-week program, so the long run is shorter and the Thursday session is easier.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
Common Race Day Nutrition Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

Over the past weeks, we’ve focused on building your race day nutrition plan. This week, let’s dive into some of the most common mistakes athletes make during endurance events—and how to steer clear of them.

1. Failing to Plan and Practice Nutrition

During a long race, your body primarily relies on fat stores for fuel. However, carbohydrates are essential to keep this “fat-burning fire” going. Most runners need 40–65 grams of carbs per hour (200–280 calories) to sustain energy levels.

How to Avoid This Mistake:

- Practice Your Nutrition Plan: Use your long training runs to identify the types and amounts of fuel your body tolerates. Too little fuel can lead to fatigue; too much can cause stomach upset.

- Mix Your Fuel Sources: Consider a combination of options: Liquids: Sports drinks from brands like Torq, Hammer, or Endura. Solids or Semi-Solids: Energy bars, gels, chews, or bloks. Real Food: Low-fiber, low-fat, low-protein items like white bread sandwiches, potatoes, bananas, or pikelets.

- Liquids: Sports drinks from brands like Torq, Hammer, or Endura.

- Solids or Semi-Solids: Energy bars, gels, chews, or bloks.

- Real Food: Low-fiber, low-fat, low-protein items like white bread sandwiches, potatoes, bananas, or pikelets.

- Know Your Course: Research what nutrition products will be available at aid stations during your race and test them in training.

2. Forgetting to Eat

Excitement and focus can make it easy to forget to fuel, especially early in the race. However, starting your fueling strategy right from the first hour is critical. Waiting until hour two or three can leave you unable to catch up.

How to Avoid This Mistake:

- Set a reminder: Use your watch to beep every 20–30 minutes as a reminder to eat or drink.

- Begin fuelling within the first hour of the race to stay ahead of your energy needs.

3. Ignoring Hydration

Hydration plays a key role in performance, but both dehydration and overhydration can be detrimental.

Before the Race:

- Hydrate moderately in the three days leading up to the race —about 2 liters per day for most people.

- Use electrolyte drinks instead of plain water to maintain sodium balance.

During the Race:

- Tailor your hydration strategy to the weather and your sweat rate. Practice this during long training runs.

- Consider carrying salt tablets to replenish sodium and reduce the risk of cramps, especially in hot or humid conditions.

4. Trying Something New on Race Day

Race day is not the time to experiment with unfamiliar foods, drinks, or routines. Even small changes can upset your stomach or throw off your performance.

How to Avoid This Mistake:

- Plan ahead: Know what you’ll eat for dinner and breakfast and ensure you have the equipment you need (e.g., toaster, fridge).

- Practice: Test your planned pre-race breakfast during training to confirm it works for you.

5. Overdoing Carb Loading with Too Much Fibre

Carb loading is crucial to ensure your glycogen stores are full, but high-fibre foods (e.g., whole grains, beans, legumes) can cause digestive issues if your gut isn’t accustomed to them.

How to Avoid This Mistake:

- Adjust your diet 3 days before the race to focus on low-fibre, high-GI carbs like white rice, pasta, and bread.

- Avoid introducing high-fibre foods if you don’t usually eat them.

- Keep your pre-race dinner and breakfast low in fibre, low in fat, high in carbs, and low in protein.

Final Thoughts

A solid nutrition plan won’t necessarily make you faster, but it will allow you to perform at your best for longer. By avoiding these common mistakes, you’ll cross the finish line feeling strong and proud of your effort. Plan ahead, practice often, and trust your preparation for a successful race day!
