Welcome to Week 13 of your Six Foot Track Training Plan

This is the final big week in the program.

This week your long run should be all about putting into practise everything you have learnt.

Once again, you should be trying to find terrain which is similar to your race course. If you haven’t done a lot of downhill running in recent weeks, then this would be a good week to focus on the downhill sections during your long run.

When you run downhill, you use your quad muscles as a brake, which causes micro tears in the muscle cells, which in turn, causes DOMs (delayed onset of muscle soreness). When your bodies repair this micro trauma (by eating healthy food and getting enough sleep), the muscle cells actually become stronger for a 4 – 6 week period.

What this means is that if you schedule a hardish downhill running session 3 weeks out from race day, your quads will be strong on race day. You will be less likely to suffer from cramp and less likely to get knee or ITB pain if you condition your legs in this way.

Please note – if you already have aches and pains in your knees then ignore this extra downhill training advice. A flatter course at an easy pace will be much a much better option for your knees.

Strength and Stability Workouts

This week we are stepping back to the 20 minute strength and stability workouts. The aim now is to maintain your strength and stability, but to reduce the total training load so that your legs will start to freshen up during the taper weeks.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 14 of your Six Foot Track Training Plan

It is taper time!

It is now time to start backing off the training volume, but it is important to try and maintain the same training frequency and pace / intensity. The idea with tapering down to an event is to freshen your legs, boost your immune system and regain some energy. However, if you stop running completely you might end up feeling “flat” and underperforming on race day.

Overcooked or Undercooked on Race Day – Which is better?

Overcooked = slightly overtrained and possibly a little under your “ideal” race weight. Undercooked = slightly undertrained and possibly a kilogram or two over your “ideal” race weight.

If you were to ask me whether or not you would be better to be overcooked or undercooked for any endurance race, my answer would always be undercooked . (NB: unless you are using it as a build up race for an upcoming longer event).

Going into an ultra-marathon undercooked doesn’t mean taking the soft/easy option and opting out of the long, hard training sessions you have planned. Nor does it mean sleeping through your alarm clock on a regular basis because you “don’t feel like training” on that particular morning.

A good example of a common mistake made by runners was evident at a Six Foot Track Marathon a few years back that I was running. I spoke to several competitors at the finish line of the event who were disappointed with their performance on race day.

A couple of them admitted it was due to generally poor training, but two seasoned athletes (who I thought would have known better) had run a 35km training run the weekend before the event as a “final hit-out”. They didn’t suffer any injuries or niggles from the run, but they were completely unaware that the fatigue caused by a long training run doesn’t disappear in 2 – 3 days. Depending on the duration and intensity of the session it can take up to 2 -3 weeks for your body to fully recover. They had unknowingly gone into the event with tired and fatigued legs and suffered the consequences by having a bad race.

If you are an experienced campaigner and have been racing ultras for a long time, then you will probably feel that you know what works best for you in terms of a taper. If that is the case, and you a racing to a level you are happy with, then you should stick with what you know.

If you have done a few ultras and feel like you have trained well, but haven’t yet had a race that you are completely happy with, then you may have got the taper wrong.

If you are new to ultras and you are not sure what to do for these last few weeks, then avoid the temptation to squeeze in “one last hard session”. It is more likely to be for mental reassurance than physical conditioning that you feel like you should do it. You are unlikely to get any fitter in the final 3 weeks, but you do have a high chance of becoming more fatigued, or worse still, injured, if you try and keep up the high volume work right through until race day.

Tapering: How to manage your last 3 weeks of training

The final 3 weeks are all about keeping your legs ticking over, keeping your brain happy that you still know how to run, and also keeping with the routine that your body has become accustomed to over the last few months of training.

If, for example, you are used to getting up at 5am most mornings to run, and with 3 weeks to go you suddenly change to “sleeping in” until 6:30am every morning, then your body is going to wonder what you are doing to it. It will probably throw your digestive system, and possibly your general motivation out of kilter and by race day you may not feel like you are “ready” to race.

It is a better idea with 3 weeks to go to maintain your frequency of running, but back off the volume. If, for example, you have been following the training plan and running 4-5 days per week, then you should continue to run 4-5 days per week

- With 3 weeks to go you reduce the total weekly volume down to about 70% of the biggest week

- With 2 weeks to go it reduces further to 45-50% of the biggest week

- In the final week , two easy 5km aerobic runs is great for the brain and not taxing on the legs.

None of these runs should be faster (or slower) than usual either. There is a common mentality in runners that their short runs need to be faster. This is certainly not the case during your taper weeks. Keep to your normal training pace and try to enjoy the fact that you have more energy than you have had recently.

Following these basic guidelines will go a long way towards ensuring you are not overcooked on race day.

Try to enjoy your taper. It is a time when a lot of people start second-guessing everything they have done:

- “Should I just do one more long run?”

- “I wish I’d done that 4 hour run my friends did a few weeks ago”

- “Should I try out that different high-carb drink that John recommended yesterday?”

- Will thicker socks be better for a long race?”

Putting it bluntly, it is too late now to change anything . What is done is done, and more importantly, what is not done – you can’t catch up on.

Enjoy your taper and give it everything you’ve got on a fresh set of legs on race day.

Get More Sleep

One of the best ways to help your body recover from the past few weeks of heavy training is to sleep more. Research shows that athletic performance improves with sufficient sleep. Rested athletes are faster. Get whatever extra sleep you can over the next 3 weeks. 30 minutes here, and 30 minutes there all counts. So sleep when you can.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
With race day just three weeks away, it’s time to fine-tune your nutrition strategy during your final weekend runs. Take the time to record each fuel source, its carbohydrate content, and how much you’ll need based on your target race time.

Practice Makes Perfect

Think about how you’ll carry your fuel on race day. With all the mandatory gear you’ll need to bring, it’s crucial to have a system in place that allows you to access your nutrition easily and on schedule. Practice this setup during your training runs to ensure it works smoothly.

Be Prepared, but Stay Flexible

Stick to the nutrition plan you’ve practiced, but remain adaptable. If you start feeling nauseous or unwell during the race, ease off the fuel for 20–30 minutes, sip water, and then gradually reintroduce your planned nutrition.

Preparation and adaptability are key to race day success!

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 15 of your Six Foot Track Training Plan

More tapering to look forward to this week.

This week sees a significant reduction in the length of the long run, and a “fairly easy” mid-week hill repeats session. The other runs remain unchanged.

By maintaining both the frequency and intensity of the runs, but dropping the total volume, it will give your legs a chance to recover from the hard training over the past 14 weeks, whilst at the same time keeping them used to ticking over. This tapering effect will also allow your immune system and overall energy levels to improve, which will have you fresh and raring to go on race day.

It is not too late to get more sleep

One of the best ways to help your body recover from the past few weeks of heavy training is to sleep more. Research shows that athletic performance improves with sufficient sleep. Rested athletes are faster. Get whatever extra sleep you can over the next 2 weeks. 30 minutes here, and 30 minutes there all counts. So sleep when you can.

Read this great ARTICLE from Runners World explaining why extra sleep in the week before your major race will pay dividends on race day.

Your Body Maintenance

You still need to keep up with your stretching and rolling routine this week. It is easy to get a bit slack with body maintenance as the training volume decreases, but it is just as important as ever. You need your muscles to be in tip-top shape on race day.

This week we are dropping back to the 10 minute workouts to help maintain your stability and complement the taper.

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
Managing Nutrition During Your Taper

As you approach race day and your training load decreases, it’s natural to experience “taper tantrums.” Your metabolism will still be in high gear, and even though your calorie expenditure from training has dropped, you may find yourself eating the same amount as before.

Stick to the Basics

Continue following the “JERF” (Just Eat Real Food) principle to maintain a strong immune system. This is not the time to compromise your health with poor dietary choices. Many runners report feeling like they’re “getting a cold” during taper week. In most cases, it’s just nerves—your body is responding to the stress of anticipation and the hard work you’ve put in to reach this point.

Balance Your Intake

If you’re prone to weight gain during periods of reduced activity, pay closer attention to your carbohydrate intake. Focus on nutrient-dense, low-carb vegetables (like those that grow above ground), lean proteins, and healthy fats to stay energised without overloading on calories.

By managing your nutrition wisely during your taper, you’ll arrive at race day feeling strong, healthy, and ready to perform!

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to Week 16. The final week of your Six Foot Track Training Plan

Congratulations on making it this far through the training program. All of the hard work is done, and this weekend you get to reap the rewards of all of that effort.

Training Advice

With only a few days to go, your legs should be feeling fresher and stronger, but you’re probably starting to question everything:

- Why are my calves so tight?

- Am I getting a cold?

- Have I done enough training?

- Dave thinks I should have gels instead of bars, I wonder if he’s right . . .

All of these questions and insecurities are a normal part of tapering. You have to trust in what you have done . And, if you haven’t done it, it is too late anyway – so there is no point in fretting about it.

Strength and Stability

This week we are dropping the strength and stability work, but maintaining the stretching and rolling.

The focus is on maintaining flexibility and mobility to help prevent your joints and muscles stiffening up over the course of this week. The reduction in training, and change in routine, can have a negative impact on your body, so it is very important to keep up with this mobility training.

NB: For any of you following the program who haven’t been doing these stretches and exercises regularly – DON’T START NOW! – Think of it like running training. If you haven’t started your running training yet, then you can’t cram it all into the final week. If you haven’t started stretching or rolling yet, then you definitely shouldn’t try to cram it all into the last week. You will do yourself far more harm than good.

Good Luck – I hope you have a great race

notes.label: Nutrition
notes.text:
What Should You Eat on Race Day?

Pre-Race Breakfast Race morning nerves are common, but avoid trying new foods or drinks. Stick to what you’ve practiced in training. Aim for a light meal 2 hours before the race, mostly carbohydrates, with around 1-2 grams of carbs per kilogram of body weight.

For example, if you weigh 60 kg, aim for 60-120 grams of carbs. If you’re short on time, go for the lower end of this range. Keep the meal low in fibre, fat, and protein to reduce the risk of digestive upset.

Examples of 30 Grams of Carbs

- 1 medium banana

- 2 slices white bread

- 1.5 crumpets

- 4-6 dates

- 2 tablespoons honey

- 1 gel (check the label, usually 20-30g)

- Sports drink (check the label)

You can also take a gel 10-15 minutes before the start if desired.

Fuelling During the Race

Hydration Hydration is a crucial part of your race day strategy but is often overlooked. The amount of water you lose during a race varies based on factors like weather and your sweat rate. If you haven’t already calculated your sweat rate, a general guideline is around 600-750 ml per hour.

Faster runners might struggle to take in enough fluids during the race, but dehydration is a serious concern. Make sure to drink at all aid stations.

Slower runners tend to drink more, but may face the risk of hyponatremia, which occurs when your sodium levels drop too low. To avoid this, consume sodium and other electrolytes during the race and avoid over-hydration.

Post-Race Recovery

After the race, if you’re still alert enough to focus on recovery, aim to refuel within 45-60 minutes of finishing, before you reach for that post-race beer.

Replenish glycogen (carbohydrates) and support muscle recovery with protein. The ideal ratio is 4:1 carbs to protein.

Sports recovery drinks or bars are great for this, as they are portable and convenient when access to a full meal may be limited. If possible, have a support crew member bring you something to refuel right after the race.

Remember, alcohol isn’t a good choice for hydration. Hydrate and refuel properly before celebrating!

glossary.definition:
For your Six Foot training plan you will see a number of shorthand descriptions which describe the details for that specific run. For example “Hill Reps” or “ELEV” or “UpDown Reps”

To use this training plan properly, and to get the most benefit from it, you need to understand what these session descriptions mean, so that you can use them to best effect in your training.

Choose your training level – Beginner, Intermediate or Advanced?

🔰 Beginner Plan This program is designed for runners who have been training consistently for at least 18 months and be comfortable running 15–16km on undulating terrain without injury. You should be able to consistently run 35-40km / week. The plan starts with manageable long runs and gradually builds your endurance, strength, and trail confidence over 16 weeks. You’ll follow a balanced mix of long runs, recovery sessions, mobility, and trail-specific strength work to prepare your body for the demands of ultra-distance running.

Beginner runners are aiming to complete the event feeling strong and in control — more of a trail adventure than a race.

⚡ Intermediate Plan This program is ideal for runners who’ve been training consistently for at least 2 years and are comfortable running 18–20km on trails. You should be able to sustain 45-50km per week of running. You’re looking to build on past performances and want to run a steady, confident 45km. Training includes structured intervals, progressive long runs, and strength and mobility sessions tailored to trail runners. You’ll also get guidance on pacing, fuelling, and recovery to help you train smarter and stay injury-free.

Intermediate runners are aiming to run the full course at a steady effort and finish with a sense of accomplishment — and maybe a personal best.

🔥 Advanced Plan This program is built for experienced ultra-distance runners who have at least 3 years of consistent training, are confident running 60 – 65km per week and are already comfortable running 22km+ regularly on trails. You’re used to weekly hill reps, tempo sessions, and longer efforts, and want to race the 45km with purpose. The plan includes hill reps, stair reps, tempo runs and sessions designed to simulate race day terrain and fatigue. Strength and mobility work are integrated to maximise performance and reduce injury risk.

Advanced runners are aiming to race Six Foot with a strong, sustained effort from start to finish.

This chart shows the long run distance and total weekly volume for each of the three levels. It can help you to choose which level of the plan is the most appropriate one to follow. It will also help you plan your long runs in advance.

Choose the level that suits your current level of fitness. e.g. if you have consistently been running 30-35km per week for the past few months then choose the beginner level. The intermediate and advanced plans will probably cause you an injury. You can always change levels during the plan if you are finding it too easy or too hard.

Session Descriptions (in alphabetical order)

Accelerations are 20 to 40 second efforts building from an easy jog to a relaxed hard effort, and then easing back down to a jog again. Focus on running tall and keeping your cadence high and your strides short. Slowly walk or jog for 1 minute between accelerations. The purpose of accelerations is improve your leg speed, hip mobility, glute strength and running technique. NB: They are not a sprinting or speedwork session.

You should be able to talk comfortably in normal sentences when running at an aerobic pace. The purpose of these sessions is to add more mileage to your week without causing too much fatigue. Aerobic runs improve your running economy to make you a more efficient runner.

A routine of exercises including stretching, stability, strengthening, foam rolling and trigger point ball. There will be regular changes to the exercises included in the routine, to focus on different body parts as required to compliment the training program. NB: These exercises are an integral part of this training program. The Body Maintenance sessions are equally as important as the running sessions.

Cross training could be swimming, cycling, elliptical, rowing, pilates or yoga or a low impact gym class. These sessions are good for your body as they use different muscle groups and are low impact. They will help to increase your aerobic fitness and endurance without the impact of increasing your running mileage. Don’t perform these sessions if you are feeling too fatigued from the current training load.

Cross training sessions can be anything from 30 mins to 90 mins in duration.

The main focus of this long run is the downhill sections of the course. Run the downhill sections of your run at race pace. Run the uphills and the flat sections at your aerobic pace. If necessary, walk / hike up the hills to help your recovery. The purpose of this run is to strengthen your quad muscles so that you can run quickly and efficiently over the first 15km downhill section of the Six Foot Track Marathon course and still have strength in your legs to run/hike strongly on the uphills.. If you have any niggles in your knees, or any ITB issues, then you should not run the downhills hard. There is too much risk of making your symptoms worse.

NB: You should try to find the longest/biggest hills possible for these runs. For example, a 5km single downhill will provide a lot more benefit than repeating a 1km downhill 5 times. This will obviously depend on the terrain you have available.

These elevation profiles are a measure of the total amount of vertical elevation during a run. Your total elevation can be measured by most current GPS watches, or you can run with your phone and download an app called Strava which will record your elevation.

The Six Foot Track course has an official elevation of 1528m , and distance of 45km. The elevation targets in the plan are set at approximately 250m of vert per 10km of running.

If you are feeling excessively tired or you are finding the training difficult, you should stick to the lower end of the vert targets, or even reduce them further. You will get more benefit from reducing the vert, but maintaining as much of the training volume as you can in order to reduce injury risk and keep your body healthy.

Pick a relatively flat course for these runs. Including a few small hills is ok. Something like 100m / 10km of running. The purpose of these flatter runs is active recovery. They help to increase your weekly mileage safely, without causing too much fatigue on your system.

Hill repeats are repeated short segments of harder uphill running. They increase aerobic power, high-intensity fatigue resistance, pain tolerance, and run-specific strength. The ideal hill on which to run hill repeats is a steady, moderate gradient of 4 to 6 percent and about 500m long. NB: During hill repeats you should be breathing hard and only able to speak 2 or 3 words at a time. BUT YOU ARE NOT SPRINTING!

I suggest you make as many of your long runs as possible on trail. Trail running is more forgiving on your body due to the variation in your stride pattern caused by the changing terrain. You are also training for a trail event, so training on trails is more race-specific.

In an ideal world you should try to make most of your long runs on terrain that is similar to the Six Foot course . This will help to condition your legs for race day, and will also give you the opportunity to practice using poles if you are intending to race with them.

On some of the long runs I have a maximum run time recommendation. For example it might be a 35km run with 800m – 1000m vert and a 4.5 hour time cap. You stop the run at 35km or 4.5 hours. Whichever comes first. These time caps are designed to help minimise the chance of you becoming fatigued or injured. The terrain you train on will have a major influence on the distance you can run in a given time.

Go to www.parkrun.com.au to learn more about Park Runs. You can replace a park run with a 5km run on the flat or small rolling hills if there isn’t a convenient park run near you, or if you prefer to run alone.

During the recovery weeks all of the runs are at aerobic pace and there is significantly less total elevation for the week. We continue with some easy accelerations during the recovery week to help maintain your leg speed and running confidence. The purpose of a recovery week is to let your body and your immune system recover. It will also help to reduce any muscle tightness and niggles. These weeks will help to restore your energy for the next training build phase. Do Not do any of these runs fast, and Please Do Not run over the stated volumes.

Rest days are vital to help your body recover from the training sessions. Without adequate rest you are more likely to become ill and injured. Try to get as much sleep and recovery time as possible on these days.

Rolling hills is the term we use to describe running over a course that is consistently going up and downhill for the duration of your run. Plan ahead and identify a course that has a good amount of up and downhill. The hills should be as regular as possible throughout the course. Consider running a short hilly loop multiple times if you don’t have access to a long hilly route. You should average approximately 200m – 400m of vertical elevation per 10km of running on rolling hills.

Find the longest staircase that you can conveniently get to for this session. The more steps the better. For these stair repeats you should be mostly hiking. You can run small sections of them if you are feeling strong, but hiking will be more race-specific. Run slowly back down the stairs slowly to recover. Repeat for the stated duration on the training plan. NB: Your pace should stay consistent throughout the session. Don’t start so fast that you can’t maintain your pace.

You should be able to talk in short sentences or a few words at a time while running at tempo pace . Think about running between 10km and half marathon race pace. The purpose of the tempo sessions is to help improve your running form, your VO2Max, and to help to keep your hips and glutes mobile and strong.

The purpose of UpDown Repeats is to improve your skill and speed at downhill running, and to strengthen your quad muscles which will help you to climb strongly after the downhill sections of the course. For these reps find a 1km section of your run route (road or fire trail) which is consistently undulating. Ideally on gentle inclines of 5 to 8 degrees. Run these reps at tempo effort (NB: your pace will vary significantly depending on whether you are running uphill or downhill, but your level of effort or perceived exertion should be consistent during the rep. For the recovery between reps you should either walk or jog slowly for 2 minutes (meaning your next rep might be in the reverse direction depending on the course you have chosen).

The main focus of this long run is the uphill sections of the course. During the second half of this run, run up the hills at tempo effort (able to talk in 3 – 4 word sentences before needing to draw breath). The purpose of this session is to increase cardio-vascular fitness, glute and calf muscle strength and improve your fatigue resistance and mental strength for race day.
